title: The Weekend Half of Korea Is on the Same Road

slides.headline: **Thirty million Koreans** leave home at once.
slides.note: Not an evacuation. Chuseok (추석) is coming, and more than half the country drives to a hometown inside the same two days.

slides.headline: Chuseok is the **harvest holiday**
slides.body: Three days when a family gathers at the oldest relative's house to set a table for the dead and eat with the living.

slides.headline: Everyone travels **one direction**
slides.body: Out of Seoul on the first day, back in on the last. Half the country lives around the capital, so the road has one shape.

slides.headline: Four hours becomes **nine**
slides.body: Seoul to Busan is a straight motorway run. On the peak morning that same drive has taken well past nine hours.

slides.headline: **won in tolls**, for three days
slides.body: Every toll in the country is waived for the three days. The state gives up the revenue to keep the queue moving.

slides.headline: Train seats go in **minutes**
slides.body: Korail opens the holiday timetable on one morning weeks ahead. The Seoul–Busan window is gone while the page is still loading.

slides.headline: The jam is **forecast in advance**
slides.body: Departure times, peak hours, hour-by-hour updates on the radio. People know exactly what it costs them, and they still go.

slides.headline: Elsewhere the holiday **spreads out**
slides.body: Thanksgiving and Christmas travel run across a week or more. Here the same crowd moves in two days, all of it one way.

slides.headline: Seoul **empties**, the towns fill
slides.body: For three days the capital goes quiet and the small places are loud. Then it all runs backwards, and that is the holiday working.

slides.headline: Korea, explained **by a Korean.**
slides.body: Follow for the context behind the things Korea does.

caption:
Next week Korea does the thing it does every autumn: around thirty million people get on the road inside two days, all of them heading the same way at once. The holiday is Chuseok, and almost everyone spends it at a hometown rather than at home.

The drive is the part nobody softens. Seoul to Busan is four hours on an ordinary Tuesday and has taken more than nine on a Chuseok morning. Motorway tolls are dropped for the whole holiday, the radio runs traffic reports through the night, and families leave at 2am to get ahead of the people who left at 4am.

What makes it strange from outside is that none of this is a surprise. The jam is announced, mapped and counted before it happens. Everyone goes anyway, because the traffic was never the point — being in the room is.
reply:
One thing that did not fit on the cards: the smart move is to leave at 2am. Families load the car around midnight, drive while the children sleep in the back, and arrive in time for breakfast. Traffic radio runs all night for exactly those drivers.

How far does your family travel for the biggest holiday of the year?
